lesson.title: Rewriting a Product as a Fraction
lesson.summary: L'Hopital's Rule only accepts fractions in the form 0/0 or infinity/infinity, so before it can touch a limit shaped like zero times infinity, that product first has to be rewritten as a quotient.
lesson.body:
A new indeterminate form arises when a product f(x) * g(x) has one factor approaching 0 and the other approaching infinity. Direct substitution gives "zero times infinity," which has no defined value: it is not obviously 0, since one factor is going to nothing, and not obviously infinite, since the other factor is exploding, and the true outcome depends entirely on which effect wins, which cannot be read off from the form alone. This is indeterminate in the same spirit as 0/0.

L'Hopital's Rule cannot be applied directly to a product, since it is stated for quotients only, so the first move is always algebraic. The identity f * g = f / (1/g), and equally g / (1/f), turns a product into a quotient. Both rewrites are mathematically valid, but they are not equally useful: one of them often leaves a much simpler derivative to compute than the other, and choosing the right one is a real skill worth practicing, not just a mechanical step.

Consider the limit as x approaches 0 from the positive side of x * ln(x). As x approaches 0 from the right, x approaches 0 while ln(x) approaches negative infinity, giving the product form 0 times negative infinity, a valid instance of the zero times infinity pattern. Rewriting as x / (1 / ln x) would leave a derivative involving 1/ln(x), which is unpleasant to differentiate. Rewriting instead as ln(x) / (1/x) is the better choice. As x approaches 0 from the right, the numerator ln(x) approaches negative infinity and the denominator 1/x approaches positive infinity, so this is now an infinity over infinity form and L'Hopital's Rule applies. Differentiating: the derivative of ln x is 1/x, and the derivative of 1/x (that is, x^-1) is -1/x^2. The new ratio is (1/x) divided by (-1/x^2), which simplifies to (1/x) * (-x^2) = -x. As x approaches 0 from the right, -x approaches 0. So the original limit equals 0.

Even though ln(x) plunges toward negative infinity, x shrinks toward 0 fast enough to pull the entire product down to exactly 0 rather than to negative infinity or to some other finite value. This particular result, x * ln(x) approaching 0 as x approaches 0 from the right, will come back directly in the chapter on indeterminate powers, where it settles the value of x^x as x approaches 0.
